title: Court, and whether he worked over or under scale
summary: In court he stayed silent about pay; he insists he always asked over scale.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: So I go to court and they read the charges and everything. Now I can't tell why we were fighting, otherwise I'm going to blow it on Sid and Ben and all three of us will get kicked out of the union. I can't open my mouth.
What, well you told me this story before, you said you were doing it under scale, is that right?
I thought you told me before that Leon-
No. I said Ben got his price, Big Sid got his price,
I mean last year when you told me about it.

No, no, no. No, not under scale, never. No, I always got over scale. I wasn't a scale musician. I never worked for scales in Chicago. Only time that I worked for scales in Chicago, in New York was Stuff Smith, my first job. And then little by little as I felt my worth, you know if they wanted me, I asked my price. If they just wanted a bass player, they'd go get someone else. This is how I found out what my worth was. Sometimes, I under played myself, you know and other times I over-rated myself too, you know. One in one hand and one in the other.

But, I went to court. And he won his suit. He said after we got outside, if anyone ask you what happened, just tell them it's a misunderstanding. He says come on over to the house and have a drink. Now, you know, I'm pouting like mad, I'm ready to blow up like a blimp, you know. I said all right. I go over to his house. He said what are you drinking? I say a glass of water, I'm afraid he going to give me a Mickey Finn, anything to get even, you know. But I didn't tell you the aftermath, after the fight.
